paper_title: CogBattery: Human-Referenced Evaluation of Cognitive Task Behavior and Structure in Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Human cognitive tasks let us compare language models with humans under controlled conditions. Yet a model can reproduce the direction of a human effect while making different errors. CogBattery evaluates 54 open-weight language models on text adaptations of 13 cognitive paradigms, comparing each with human data from its source study. Like humans, models respond more to n-back lures than to controls, yet they make far more false alarms on ordinary non-targets. Most models' reported confidence separates correct from incorrect answers less well than humans' does, and most always choose the same wager, including models that classify accurately. These patterns span many model families. Across tasks, model scores share two dimensions. The first is closely tied to scale, yet larger models are not consistently closer to humans. Predefined cognitive groupings show no reliable predictive advantage over random groupings of the same size. These results show that matching human effect directions does not establish human-like behavior. CogBattery provides condition-level human references for testing errors and confidence reports in new models.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Human cognitive tasks compare conditions that differ in controlled way, and published human data show how people respond in each. They therefore allow direct comparisons between language models and humans and reveal errors hidden by aggregate accuracy (Coda-Forno et al., 2024; Binz and Schulz, 2023; Momentè et al., 2025). model that shows human condition effect, such as decision bias (Binz and Schulz, 2023; Itzhak et al., 2024), can look human-like. But matching the direction of an effect does not mean making the same errors or reports. models confidence can be higher on correct than on incorrect answers, as peoples is, yet separate the two less well. Studies of decision making, n-back, and executive function show that shared effects can mask different errors, sensitivities, and confidence reports (Coda-Forno et al., 2024; Hu and Lewis, 2025; de Langis et al., 2026), but each covers few paradigms or few models  (Table 1)  , so how general these differences are remains unclear. CogBattery evaluates 54 open-weight models from 23 families on text adaptations of 13 paradigms (Figure 1). No human cohort covers all 13 paradigms, so each paradigm is compared with source-specific published human data, mostly participant-level records, by condition and response type  (Table 2)  . We also check whether differences hold among models that reach minimal level on each task and whether they vary with model size. The paradigms fall into five groups by origin, such as working memory and metacognition, and we test whether these groups predict held-out families task scores better than random groups of equal size. Task correlations need the same people on several tasks, and robust condition effects do not guarantee reliable individual differences (Hedge et al., 2018), so structure is compared only in four such cohorts (Eisenberg et al., 2019; Ball et al., 2022; Poldrack et al., 2016; Bradford et al., 2020). Our findings are as follows. First, shared directions hide different errors. The n-back lure effect sits on many false alarms to ordinary non-targets, an excess of .257 over humans, and Stroop interference is much larger than humans (Figure 2, Table 4). Second, verbal confidence separates correct from incorrect answers less well than humans does, although token probabilities do about as well, and most models always choose the same wager. Third, several gaps remain among gate passers, and the n-back excess remains in models of 27B or Figure 1: Overview of CogBattery. Panel 2B tests whether task groups add value in family-held-out prediction. more  (Table 5)  . Fourth, model scores share scalerelated dimension, yet larger models are not consistently closer to humans (Figure 3), and predefined groups add no reliable predictive value over random groups. Comparisons with humans thus need errors and confidence reports, not only effect directions. CogBattery enables such comparisons for new models, with the same text materials, condition-level human references, and scorers used here.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Cognitive tasks and human-referenced behavior. Several evaluations port cognitive tasks to language models. CogBench separates performance from behavior (Coda-Forno et al., 2024), CogEval tests cognitive claims with controls (Momennejad et al., 2023), and triangulation links cognitive tests, games, and benchmarks (Momentè et al., 2025). Others predict human choices directly (Binz et al., 2025). Single-paradigm studies show that instruction tuning can strengthen human-like decision biases (Itzhak et al., 2024). Working-memory and executive-function studies probe capacity and control (Gong et al., 2024; de Langis et al., 2026), n-back failures can reflect task misunderstanding rather than capacity (Hu and Lewis, 2025), and cumulative state tracking ties working-memory difficulty to the number of sequential updates (Hou et al., 2026). Direct human comparisons find differences within shared effect directions. Visual Stroop shows different error curves (Patel et al., 2026), confidence differences depend on the task (Cash et al., 2026), and GPT-4 has lower AUROC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) than humans on four-choice but not twochoice Japanese general knowledge (Yoshizawa et al., 2026). Some models use confidence to guide abstention (Kumaran et al., 2026). The evaluations in Table 1 cover few paradigms or few models, and they use human data only as norms or scaling constants, if at all. CogBattery asks how widely specific errors and confidence reports recur, comparing 54 models from 23 families with human data from each paradigms source study. Text adaptations and auxiliary demands constrain interpretation (Hu and Frank, 2024), and protocol differences preclude matched comparisons to published model scores. Profiles and task-score structure. Profiling systems use cognitive labels (Zhou et al., 2026; Haznitrama et al., 2026; Cui et al., 2026). Filled circles mark reported analyses and open circles unreported ones. Family-held-out prediction tests families absent from training. Human and model task correlations are compared in jointly measured subsets. CogBenchs count follows the proceedings. soning, and metacognition (Miyake et al., 2000; Wellman et al., 2001; Lichtenstein and Fischhoff, 1977). Benchmark factor studies motivate testing shared variation, scale, and incremental prediction (Burnell et al., 2023; Ilic and Gignac, 2024; Kipnis et al., 2025). Condition effects do not guarantee reliable individual differences (Hedge et al., 2018), and task convergence and construct validity require separate evidence (Trott et al., 2026; Bean et al., 2025; Jung et al., 2026). We therefore test whether these paradigm-origin groups add predictive value for task scores in held-out model families.

sections.title: 3 Battery and Administration
sections.content: 3.1 Tasks and human references Table 2 defines the tasks and their five groups, and Table 3 gives the score of each task used in the structure analyses. Each task is compared with human data from its source study, and most of these are participant-level records. For DS, ST, FL, and GN the models replay three public trial sequences of Self-Regulation Ontology (SRO) participants (Eisenberg et al., 2019), and NB uses 80 participantmatched blocks. CVLT uses 130 healthy Consortium for Neuropsychiatric Phenomics (CNP) controls on the CVLT-II Standard lists, with all 272 records in sensitivity analysis (Delis et al., 2000; Poldrack et al., 2016). Table 2 names the sources for the other tasks (Ball et al., 2022; Eerland and Zwaan, 2018; Strachan et al., 2024; Jones et al., 2024; Mazancieux et al., 2020), and each CAL item appears in both answer orders. Two references are weaker. OS reconstructs Balls rules with different item orders, and WAG has only published grammar strings and human summaries (Dienes and Scott, 2005; Dienes and Seth, 2010). Example item. For 2-back, 1:G 2:V 3:g requires MATCH because the current letter matches two positions earlier, ignoring case. Earlier letters and the models earlier answers stay visible. 3.2 Model panel and execution The 54 open-weight models span 23 families, merging versions of the same series (28 raw labels), and 0.36B141B total parameters, including all mixture-of-experts parameters. Families include Qwen, Llama, Gemma, and Mistral. Sensitivity panels retain prespecified 19 models in nine families or the 51 direct-answer models in 22 families. All models share prepared tasks and validity rules. Qwen3 4B and DeepSeek-R1 (7B and 14B) use native thinking. The other 51 answer directly. Temperature is zero, with one response per step. Formats are constrained except free-response FB. Models are served with Ollama 0.18.0. Contexts are 4,096 tokens, or 12,288 with 8,192 output tokens for native thinking, and OS allows 128 output tokens for every model. 3.3 Response validity and behavioral coverage All 702 cells completed, giving 366,606 records including non-outcome steps. Of these, 366,248 are valid and scorable, 120 are technically invalid, 238 are valid but unparsed, and none were left unrun, so 366,486 (99.97%) are technically valid. Technical validity concerns response format and delivery, not behavioral correctness. The 238 unparsed replies are FB answers without an extracted location, and they count as wrong. Invalid task answers count as wrong, including misses on signal trials and false alarms on noise trials, without coverage gate. NB has no invalid answers, so its false-alarm rates do not depend on this rule. No human cohort covers all 13 tasks, but two cohorts did several within-group tasks. SRO supplies 345 people with DS, NB, ST, FL, and GN, and Ball supplies 409 with OS, DRM, and SM (236 unwarned, 173 warned). Ball SM matches the model task only at task-family level. In SRO and Ball, and in model scores, δ is the mean Pearson correlation of within-group task pairs minus that of between-group pairs. Larger δ means stronger relative grouping, not higher ability. SRO has 4 within-group and 6 between-group pairs, and Ball has 1 and 2. Human-minus-model differences in δ use independent 5,000-draw bootstraps over people and over model families. Missing human and invalid model answers count as wrong. 4.3 Model dimensions and prediction This step asks how many dimensions model scores share and whether paradigm groups predict scores in unseen model families. One structural score per task  (Table 3)  gives 13-column matrix for all 54 models in 23 families. Key endpoints are often contrasts with mixed directions, undefined values, and low reliability (Hedge et al., 2018), so structure uses performance scores. The original wager contrast covers only 17 models. Principal component analysis (PCA) of task correlations, 5,000-permutation parallel analyses, and minimum-residual (MINRES) factor analysis with oblimin rotation describe model profiles and family centroids. Factor intervals refit 2,000 whole-family resamples, and failed, improper, and boundary fits are counted, not replaced. For prediction we leave out one family at time. Using only the training families centroids, we fit standardization, the first principal component (PC1) of the other 12 tasks, and the residualized mean of the same-group tasks, then predict the heldout family. The ridge penalty is fixed at 106, target scores never enter the features, and root-meansquare error (RMSE) weights each familytarget cell equally. Gain is 1RMSEextended/RMSEaxis, with 20,000 paired family-error-block draws conditional on saved predictions. All 600,600 partitions of the tasks into groups of sizes 3, 3, 3, 2, and 2 give reference, and PC1+PC2 and two-factor scores are further controls.

Models do better than humans on long forward lists (length 9, .750 versus .327) and worse on short backward ones (length 3, .611 versus .961), so their forwardbackward gap is much larger. With the history visible, these are not capacity estimates. Operation-span accuracy is lower in models overall, but not among length-3 gate passers. In 2-back, both populations respond MATCH more often to lures than to controls, but models also accept many ordinary non-targets. They require above-chance accuracy (one-sided binomial < .05) on congruent FL and ST, EP control order 1, and overall SM, CAL, and WAG, hits above false alarms (one-sided Fisher < .05) on NB 2-back, GN, and unwarned DRM, or at least half correct on DS and OS length 3, CVLT trial 1, and FB true belief. Congruent ST and FL can be passed by reading words or flankers, so gates do not establish comprehension. Eleven tasks share gate and endpoint trials, and gates built from separate trials give similar gaps (Flanker .341.352, OS .057.070, CAL .140 to .061). Among gate passers, the n-back false-alarm excess and the lower AUROC remain  (Table 5)  . Passing gate does not mean performing well, though. Of the 32 n-back gate passers, 19 have balanced accuracy below .60, and only three, all nativethinking, reach .80. Constant wagers persist in 15 of 24 above-chance grammar classifiers, including four of the five scoring at least .80. Larger models narrow some gaps but not all. Among the nine models of 27B or more, the nback excess remains (.351 [.095,.644], 7 of 9). Their Stroop interference (.043 [.031, .142]) and AUROC (.026 [.140, .101]) gaps are smaller, with wide intervals. Family-clustered mixed models with log parameters and native thinking give an AUROC slope of .123 per tenfold increase [.060,.187]. The false-alarm slope (.167) is not reliably nonzero (likelihood-ratio = .06, Wald lower bound .0005), nor is the interference slope. On seven of the 13 tasks, more than 70% of models lie over one human SD from the human mean, and this distance does not shrink consistently with size (Figure 3). sections.title: 6 Score Structure
sections.content: Secondary structure analyses use 54 models in 23 families with no missing cells. Joint human cohorts with grouping contrasts are SRO (five tasks, 345 people) and Ball (three measures, 409). and variation Shared scale. Principalcomponent and common-factor parallel analyses both retain two dimensions, in models and in family centroids. Model-level PC1 explains 39.23% of standardized variance and correlates with log parameter count (r = .797, and .839 within multi-model families), as in benchmark factor and scaling studies (Burnell et al., 2023; Ilic and Gignac, 2024; Ruan et al., 2024). Residualizing every task on log size lowers PC1 to 27.00% but still leaves two dimensions, as does dropping WAG, whose constant wagers score .5 (post hoc). The first rotated factor loads broadly across origin groups. The second rotated factor contrasts NB and FL with WAG and CVLT. It is unstable under family resampling (median congruence .938 [.421,.995]). It has no reliable association with three prespecified response-bias indicators, NB control false alarms, constant wagers, and highwager rate (Spearman ρ from .23 to .12, all intervals spanning zero). Two secondary associations, with GN false alarms (.47) and CVLT false alarms (.42), are negative, and none establishes general response-bias reading. The second components eigenvalue only modestly exceeds the permutation reference (2.22 versus 1.82). Adding PC2 to PC1 gives no reliable prediction gain (3.17% [1.53, 15.73]%). With the 12 key endpoints instead, parallel analysis retains one dimension and the five groups give no reliable gain (2.02% [5.10, .48]%). Predefined groups and random groups. Adding same-group information to PC1 baseline in family-held-out prediction lowers RMSE from 1.563 to 1.515 (3.02% [5.85, 6.01]%). Of all 600,600 same-size random groupings, 14.62% do at least as well. Withinand between-group correlations are similar (δ = .021 [.085, .066]). Model split or form reliability is .869.999 except for WAG (.515). Reliability correction leaves δ = .011 [.078, .075]. The predefined groups therefore show no reliable predictive advantage, which is not evidence that they are equivalent to random groups. post hoc positive control asks whether this test can detect grouping of human size, simulating 100 score matrices per group strength. With population δ near the SRO estimate of .16, at most 5% of random groupings match the predefined one in 97 of the 100 matrices, although the gain interval excludes zero in only 26. Two alternative groupings of the same sizes, chosen after the formal results, give no reliable gain either. Grouping by response format (span, detection, labelled choice, mind stories, confidence) gives 4.63% [6.58, 8.52]%, and grouping chosen within each fold from trainingfamily correlations gives 0.80% [4.10, 11.68]%. The test concerns these 13 text-adapted paradigms, so it cannot show that models lack such abilities. Human cohorts. In SRO, the human grouping contrast exceeds the models (δH = .158, δM = .022), but the difference, .180 [.102, .371], spans zero, also after reliability correction. Model reliabilities are at least .972, so the weak model working-memory correlation (.076 versus .317 in humans) is not explained by low reliability. In Ball, the comparison depends on DRM scoring. Native false-alarm scoring gives difference of .249 [.064,.402], but both groups contrasts are negative. With pooled 56-probe accuracy the difference spans zero. Pooled balanced accuracy gives .493 [.195,.704], with positive intervals in both warning groups (.423 [.133,.651] without and .561 [.231,.810] with warning). In two further cohorts covering CVLT and FB, model correlations exceed human ones in five of six task pairs, reliably only for DSST (.44 in models versus .06 in humans). Bradford measures are adjusted for age.

sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.content: Effect directions and errors. Sharing human effect direction does not mean making human errors. In n-back the lure effect sits on top of many false alarms to ordinary letters, and in Stroop models often answer with the word instead of the color label. These task-specific patterns recur across many families, but they need not share one cause. Confidence reports. Most models confidence reports separate correct from incorrect answers less well than humans do. Their token probabilities discriminate about as well as human reports, so the gap lies in the verbal report rather than in missing correctness signal (Kadavath et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024; Steyvers et al., 2025). Neither measure shows that models use confidence to control behavior (Kumaran et al., 2026). Constant wagers mostly follow response labels, so they reflect label preference more than confidence. Gates and scale. Several differences persist above minimal-performance gates. Larger models close some gaps, but distance from humans does not shrink consistently with size (Figure 3). The gaps describe this panel of models, not fixed properties of language models. Structure and cognitive interpretation. Model scores share broad, scale-related dimension and weaker, unstable second one not reliably tied to response bias. Grouping tasks by origin adds no reliable predictive value, so the labels describe paradigm origins, not established model abilities. Implications for evaluation. Human comparisons should report errors by condition, not only effect directions. Confidence should be read from verbal reports and token probabilities, which can disagree. Wagers need counterbalanced labels, or they may measure label preference. Per-model distances from humans show what panel means hide.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Across 54 models and 13 paradigms, models often share human effect directions while differing in errors and confidence reports. These differences span many families, and larger models are not consistently closer to humans. Predefined cognitive groups lack reliable predictive advantage over random groupings of the same size, and alternative groupings add no reliable gain either, so behavioral measurements should be kept separate from cognitive interpretations. CogBattery lets new models be tested against the same condition-level human references. Model replies will be released upon publication, apart from those limited by material licenses.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: No humans were tested on the text versions, so humanmodel differences combine adaptation and population differences. Each model gives one temperature-zero response per step, so response distributions are not estimated. Closed models were not tested. Joint human cohorts cover ten tasks, so CAL, EP, and WAG have no human structural comparison, and the CNP and Bradford tasks match the model tasks only at task-family level. Published materials may occur in training data, and we ran no contamination test. Standardized distances depend on human variability, so tasks with large personlevel spread (SM, EP) or ceiling scores in both groups (FB) look closer. Of the 104 intervals across all endpoints that exclude zero with human means fixed, 95 still do when human sampling error is added. The SM difference in Table 4 is one that no longer does. The small five-group gain depends on WAG, CAL, and the deepseek-r family. Whether these patterns hold for other paradigms needs prospective test.
